description: We are an ambitious team participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, developing an innovative Space Mission Design Game that combines space exploration, strategy, and real-world science. Our goal is to create an engaging, educational, and scientifically accurate experience. We're looking for creative, motivated teammates skilled in programming, game development, UI/UX design, or 3D modelling who share our passion for innovation and space exploration.
summary: Perilune is a Windows desktop game that lets students plan, build, fly, and operate a space mission. Its showcase, Hellas Survey, starts with a rocket and rover the player can assemble in a 3D hangar. After launching from Earth, the player follows a computed N-body trajectory to Mars, manages atmospheric descent, and drives a rover through the Hellas basin. The objective is to survey two sites and relay at least 0.20 GB of science data to Earth. The game uses NASA JPL Horizons orbital states, Viking imagery, and Mars Global Surveyor laser-altimeter elevations. Perilune addresses the challenge by connecting choices about budget, fuel, instruments, power, and communications across one playable mission. Students can see how a decision made in the hangar affects whether their science ever reaches Earth.
details:
Perilune Project Details

Perilune is a 3D Windows desktop game in which players design, fly, and operate a space mission. We built it for the Space Mission Design Game challenge so students can see how a decision made during assembly affects what happens on the launch pad, in flight, and when a science team is waiting for data. The showcase mission, Hellas Survey, asks players to launch from Earth, land a rover in Hellas Planitia on Mars, survey two sites, and relay at least 0.20 GB of science data to Earth.

The challenge and the player experience

Space mission design asks teams to satisfy several constraints at once. An instrument may answer a useful science question while increasing mass, cost, and power demand. A spacecraft that reaches the correct orbit may still miss its data goal if it spends too much time in eclipse or out of radio contact. Perilune puts those relationships in the same game so players can follow a choice from its immediate cost to its effect on mission success.

The mission archive contains Hellas Survey and 15 Earth and lunar missions. A preset establishes an objective and requirements before the player enters the hangar. Earth and lunar scenarios ask the player to use specified instruments, reach an assigned orbit, and return data. Sandbox lets the player set the objective, target body, orbit, experiment, budget, mission lifetime, and return target for a custom orbital flight. It also offers a separate Mars descent practice scenario at Jezero.

Hellas Survey begins with a working stock design that players can inspect and modify. In Auto mode, assistance flies ascent, calculates and executes departure, and advances the computed coast to Mars. In Manual mode, players choose launch timing and parking altitude, control the rocket, plan departure, and command course corrections. Both modes expose telemetry and use the same force model. The two modes let a first-time player complete the full design-to-science sequence while giving practiced players responsibility for individual maneuvers.

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"The Hellas assembly bay shows fitted parts, the mission cap, and fuel for each flight phase." ]

The Hellas assembly bay shows fitted parts, the mission cap, and fuel for each flight phase.

 

Engineering decisions and resource limits

The rocket and rover have separate assembly tabs. In the rocket bay, players drag parts onto compatible mounts, remove fitted hardware, and undo changes. The catalog includes core and upper-stage engines, tanks, and solid or liquid side boosters. Fuel load, thrust, and dry mass affect liftoff and performance. A solid booster continues burning after ignition until exhausted or jettisoned. Liquid engines respond to throttle. Fairing and stage separation visibly remove hardware as the simulation removes its mass.

In the rover bay, players choose a chassis, heat shield, parachute, powered descent system, power source, and radio. Scientific instruments include a panoramic camera, a mineral spectrometer, a core sampler, and a weather station. Players can add or remove instruments and see the cost and entry mass change. A larger rover can carry more resources, but its mass also changes what the launcher, parachute, and descent engine must handle.

The stock Hellas architecture costs $159 million against a fictional $170 million mission cap. The assembly screen shows $40 million for the Earth launcher, $34 million for the cruise stage, and $85 million for the rover and landing systems. The game checks the cap before the Hellas launcher rolls out. Players can test a trade-off by choosing a higher-rate radio or another instrument and seeing how much budget and mass margin remains for the rest of the vehicle.

The launcher, cruise stage, and landing hardware have independent propellant accounts. The cruise stage and its 2,450 kg of stock propellant ride under the fairing and contribute to ascent mass. That fuel is available at Earth departure after the launcher has spent most of its own propellant. The stock landing system carries another 118 kg for powered descent. The flight display identifies which tank is in use and shows the cruise burn’s calculated effect on remaining fuel.

Power and communications introduce a different constraint on the surface. Solar generation varies with the modeled light cycle, battery charge buffers demand, and a faster radio can draw more power. Adding a spectrometer changes the science the rover can do. The observations also take power and create data that compete for recorder space and a relay pass. A player can respond by changing hardware, spacing out operations, or deciding which experiment to run first.

 

Flight physics and the Hellas landing site

The game loads a fixed NASA JPL Horizons snapshot for the Sun, eight planets, and Moon at 00:00 TDB on November 14, 2026. These starting positions and velocities are geometric vectors in the J2000 ecliptic frame, relative to the solar system barycenter. The simulation advances the bodies with mutual Newtonian gravity. During the Mars transfer, a fourth-order Runge–Kutta integrator propagates the spacecraft as a test particle under their combined gravitational acceleration.

A coarse transfer estimate gives the numerical targeting solver a starting point. The orbital map shows the resulting forecast and the trajectory actually flown. A player who changes a departure or makes a correction changes the spacecraft’s velocity and spends propellant according to the rocket equation. The game then integrates the changed trajectory. Time warp advances that calculation. This lets players see why a small correction early in cruise can change where the spacecraft encounters Mars.

We placed the target at 32.91015625° S, 62.19921875° E in Hellas Planitia. The target elevation is −8,208 m relative to the MOLA areoid, the reference surface used for these Mars elevations. It is the lowest median elevation identified in our regional scan and matches the minimum reported in the source product label. A simple pressure estimate based on NASA’s Mars Fact Sheet gives approximately 1,340 Pa at the target. That value is a modeled reference pressure. Atmospheric pressure varies with conditions and season, and MOLA measures elevation.

The low basin makes atmospheric braking a useful part of the mission design. It also exposes the vehicle to aerodynamic and thermal loads that must stay within the limits of the chosen hardware. At the 125 km interface, the arrival state supplies vertical and horizontal speeds for the descent simulation. A layered CO₂ atmosphere determines how density changes with height. The game uses that density, vehicle speed, and the deployed hardware to calculate drag and estimate heating. As the vehicle slows, the player can deploy the parachute, release the heat shield, and use the descent engine. Terrain elevation affects when the vehicle reaches the ground. Timing and equipment choices can lead to a hard landing or a failed entry.

 

Rover operations learning and verification

On approach, players see a curved Mars globe textured with Viking imagery. On the surface, a 3D driving view and a top-down traverse map share the same rover position and route. Mars Global Surveyor’s laser altimeter supplies regional elevations. The regional map shows Viking orbital imagery and marks the landing target and rover. The closer traverse view shows the science sites, waypoints, and local hazards. We simulate rover-scale rocks and relief because the regional elevation cells are hundreds of meters across.

The player drives to a site, stops, and runs a fitted instrument. The rover stores observations in its recorder. A camera survey, a mineral observation, a cached core, or a modeled weather reading requires the player to choose suitable equipment and reach an appropriate location. Power demand, storage capacity, and travel time shape what can be done before the next pass. Data leaves the rover when the modeled relay is in view and reaches Earth after a delay based on signal travel time. The science journal and telemetry let players track observations and distinguish stored, in-transit, and delivered data.

We used C# and .NET Framework with Windows Presentation Foundation for the desktop interface, interactive map, and 3D views. A PowerShell script builds the 64-bit Windows executable. The release runs offline with the source data files packaged alongside it. A verification mode exercises the flight and science models. The 15 original Earth and lunar scenarios passed their launch-to-science checks. A stock Hellas run reached the 125 km Mars interface after a 270.47-day simulated transfer at 5.95 km/s. It had about 442 kg of cruise fuel after departure and 106 kg in the separate landing tank at touchdown. The rover drove to two field sites, made observations, and returned 0.200 GB through the modeled communications path.

The educational goal is to make revision part of mission design. A student can change one subsystem and trace the effect through liftoff mass, available maneuvers, landing, and data return. A successful run demonstrates that the systems worked together for an objective. An unsuccessful run gives the student a specific constraint to investigate, such as fuel margin, entry loads, a missed observation window, or a full recorder.

NASA and JPL sources

Data loaded by the game and values used in models

Solar system states and constants. The bundled Horizons vector snapshot initializes the gravity model. Published parameters supply gravitational constants and Earth and Moon dimensions. The nominal Mars orientation is used for surface targeting. JPL Horizons · Horizons API · JPL astrodynamic constants · Planet parameters · Satellite parameters · NASA Mars orientation reference

Mars elevations. The Hellas crop comes from MOLA MEGDR product MEGT00N000HB.IMG at 128 pixels per degree. The fallback is MEGT90N000CB.IMG at 4 pixels per degree. The regional observation counts were consulted during site review. NASA PDS MOLA data and product index · Global 4 pixels per degree files · MOLA data specification

Mars images. The Hellas map uses the Viking VIS color mosaic layer Mars_Viking_MDIM21_ClrMosaic_global_232m, tile level 7, row 87, column 172. The globe uses the JPL/USGS Viking texture. The Jezero practice scenario displays the Perseverance Mastcam-Z image PIA24485. NASA Mars Trek layer catalog · JPL Viking globe texture · NASA Jezero Delta photo

Earth and Moon images. NASA Goddard’s Blue Marble composite textures Earth. The bundled JPEG from the credited mirror is unchanged. The Moon uses the 2048 × 1024 Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera color map in NASA’s CGI Moon Kit. NASA Blue Marble record · Earth JPEG and credits · CC BY-SA 3.0 · NASA CGI Moon Kit

Mars atmospheric inputs. NASA’s Mars Fact Sheet supplies the reference pressure and scale height. The Mars 2020 paper informs the representative atmosphere. NASA Mars Fact Sheet · Mars 2020 atmospheric analysis

Engineering and mission design references

Propulsion and entry. NASA Glenn thrust equation · Specific impulse · Drag equation · NASA entry heating and thermal protection · How We Land on Mars · Curiosity arrival sequence · Kepler fairing separation

Mission architecture. NASA Mission Design Lab and CubeSat 101 informed the treatment of system trade-offs and ground operations. Artemis I informed the lunar flight sequence. Perilune computes its own paths. NASA Mission Design Lab · NASA CubeSat 101 · Artemis I timeline · Artemis I trajectory operations
